Trabzon'un Şalpazarı ilçesinde taşkın ve heyelan meydana geldi
Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Malatya ve Eskişehir'deki askeri helikopter kazalarına ilişkin, "Sadece 12 gün arayla yaşanan bu iki elim kazanın araştırılmasına yönelik tahkikatlar başlatılmıştır. Bu inceleme ve araştırmalar en küçük bir şüpheye mahal bırakmayacak şekilde tüm yönleriyle yapılacaktır." dedi.
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, Beştepe Millet Kongre ve Kültür Merkezi'nde "Kadına Yönelik Şiddete Karşı Uluslararası Mücadele Günü" programında yaptığı konuşmada, dün Eskişehir'de eğitim uçuşu sırasında kaza kırıma uğrayan Hava Kuvvetlerine ait helikopterde şehit olan kahraman askerlere Allah'tan rahmet niyaz etti.
Şehitlerin kederli ailelerine, yakınlarına, silah arkadaşlarına ve Türk Silahlı Kuvvetlerine sabır dileyen, taziyelerini sunan Erdoğan, şunları söyledi:
"Malum, 12 Kasım'da Malatya Yeşilyurt'ta bir başka askeri helikopterimiz kaza kırıma uğramış, 4 askerimiz şehit düşmüştü. Sadece 12 gün arayla yaşanan bu iki elim kazanın araştırılmasına yönelik tahkikatlar başlatılmıştır. Bu inceleme ve araştırmalar en küçük bir şüpheye mahal bırakmayacak şekilde tüm yönleriyle yapılacaktır. Rabb'im şehitlerimizin ruhlarını şad, mekanlarını inşallah cennet eylesin. Rabb'im kahraman ordumuzun kahraman mensuplarının ayağına taş değdirmesin, onları her türlü kazadan, beladan muhafaza buyursun."
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, Anadolu'nun vatan yapılmasında milletin bin türlü badireyi atlatıp hayatta kalmasında büyük emeği, fedakarlığı olan ama çoğunun ismi bilinmeyen kadın kahramanları rahmetle yad etti.
Elleri öpülesi şehit anneleri başta olmak üzere milletin bekası, birliği, dirliği, ülkenin ve devletin istiklali için canlarından can veren bütün kadınlara şükranlarını sunan Erdoğan, şunları kaydetti:
"Bir insanlık suçu olan kadına yönelik şiddet olaylarında hayatlarını kaybeden hanım kardeşlerimizin her birine Cenabıallah'tan rahmet diliyor, geride bıraktıklarına sabırlar temenni ediyorum. Aynı şekilde şiddete maruz kalmış tüm kadınlara geçmiş olsun diyorum. Gazze'de, Batı Şeria'da, Lübnan'da ve komşumuz İran'da siyonist rejimin insanlık dışı şiddetinin kurbanı olan tüm kadınlara, çocuklara Allah'tan rahmet niyaz ediyor, yaralı kardeşlerimize acil şifalar temenni ediyorum. Bu salondaki siz kıymetli misafirlerimizin yanı sıra, ülkemizde ve dünyanın farklı köşelerinde kadına karşı şiddetle mücadeleye omuz veren herkese en içten tebriklerimi, takdirlerimi, teşekkürlerimi iletiyorum. Bu mücadeleyi, kimliklerin ötesinde bir insanlık mücadelesi olarak gören ve destekleyen herkesten Allah razı olsun."
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, şiddetin, dünyanın neresinde olursa olsun, kime yönelik olursa olsun kötü olduğunu, lanetlenmesi gerektiğini ifade ederek, "Kadına yönelik şiddet, çok net söylüyorum, vicdansızlıktır, insafsızlıktır, insanlıktan nasibini almamışlara mahsus bir alçaklıktır." dedi.
"Tabii burada şu ayrıma da dikkat çekmek durumundayım: Şiddet sadece kadına el kaldırmak, ona vurmak, cebri ve fiili müdahalede bulunmak değildir. Şiddetin görüneni olduğu gibi çok daha sinsi, çoğu zaman fark edilmeyen, sessizce hayatları karartan biçimleri de vardır. Mesela bir kadını sırf cinsiyeti nedeniyle ayrımcılığa maruz bırakmak, onu hor görmek, aşağılamak, iradesini yok saymak bir şiddet türüdür. Kadının emeğini sömürmek, alın terini değersizleştirmek, kadını bir meta olarak görmek şiddetin bir türüdür. Kadınları sosyal hayattan, ekonomik hayattan, bilhassa en temel hakları olan eğitimden yoksun bırakan her uygulama bir şiddet türüdür. Kadınlar üzerinde, siyasi görüşü, inancı, kutsal değerleri, hayat tarzı veya kılık kıyafeti sebebiyle psikolojik baskı kurmak bir şiddet türüdür. Özellikle son dönemde küresel bir dayatmaya dönüşen cinsiyetsizleştirme politikaları da mağdurları farklılık gösteren bir şiddet türüdür."
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, şiddetin hep fiilde değil, bazen bir kötü sözde, bazen bir tehditte, bazen de kadının hayallerinin önüne konulan engellerde kendisini gösterebildiğini dile getirdi.
"Şiddetin şekli, formu, biçimi, kişiden kişiye değişebilir ama şiddetin kadın ruhunda ve insanlık vicdanında açtığı derin yara asla değişmez. Onun için kadına yönelik şiddetin hiçbir bahanesi, hiçbir gerekçesi olamaz." değerlendirmesinde bulunan Erdoğan, sözlerini şöyle sürdürdü:
“Biz 'Şiddete Sıfır Tolerans' derken meseleye işte bu zaviyeden bakıyoruz. Ayrımcılık yapmıyor, ne şekilde tezahür ederse etsin ve kimden gelirse gelsin şiddetin her türlüsünü lanetliyoruz. Bizim mücadelemiz şiddetin sadece fiziki boyutuyla sınırlı değildir. Bizim mücadelemiz, kadını değersiz gören, emeğini, alın terini yok sayan, kadınlık onurunu zedeleyen bütün anlayışlarla, bütün uygulamalarladır. Şiddetin ortaya çıkmasını engellemeye dönük bütün politikalara ne kadar önem veriyorsak, şiddeti doğuran zihniyetle, ayrımcılıkla, istismarla, eşitsizlikle mücadeleyi de kadına yönelik şiddetle mücadelemizin asli unsuru olarak görüyoruz. Kadına yönelik şiddetle uluslararası mücadele günü olan 25 Kasım'da siz kıymetli misafirlerimizin huzurunda şunu tekrar teyit etmek isterim: Siyasi hayatı boyunca daima kadınlarla yol yürümüş, en başta eşi ve kızları olmak üzere hep kadınların desteğini görmüş, her platformda kadınların haklarını cesaretle savunmuş ve bu süreçte kimi zaman haksız eleştirilere maruz kalmış bir siyasetçi olarak bugüne kadar olduğu gibi bundan sonra da kadına karşı şiddetle mücadelenin sancaktarlığı yapmayı sürdüreceğim.”
Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan, "Güvenlik ve istihbarat birimlerimiz tespit, takip ve teyit görevlerini büyük bir hassasiyetle yerine getiriyor. Bütün adımlarımızı hukuk içinde, kararlılıkla ve devlet ciddiyetiyle atıyoruz." dedi.
"İstismara ve provokasyona açık en ufak bir alan bırakmak istemiyoruz"
"Bir anne evladının üzerine nasıl titrerse biz de bu sürecin üzerine aynı hassasiyetle titriyoruz. Amacımız huzurun, kardeşliğin, güvenliğin ve kalkınmanın güçlenmesidir"
"Biz ülkemizde annelerin gözyaşı artık dinsin, anneler, babalar, çocuklar artık gözyaşı dökmesin, fidan gibi delikanlılar hayatlarının baharında göğekin gibi toprağa düşmesin istiyoruz"
"Türkiye Yüzyılını önce Terörsüz Türkiye, ondan sonra da terörsüz bölge ile taçlandırmak istiyoruz"
"Hiç kimsenin parti içi iktidar kavgasını sürece yüklemeye, sürecin sırtına bindirmeye, sürecin önüne geçirmeye hakkı yoktur"
"Biz halisane niyetlerle hareket ettikçe kimi muhalefet partileri çözümü ertelemeye, engellemeye çalışıyorlar. Maalesef Terörsüz Türkiye sürecini kendilerine perde yapıyorlar"
"Türkiye'nin önünde 40 yıllık sorunu kalıcı biçimde çözme noktasında tarihi bir fırsat penceresi açılmıştır. Cumhur İttifakı olarak bu fırsatın heba edilmesine, kişisel kaprislere kurban edilmesine izin vermeyiz"

Terminal Kadıköy’deki Paribu Art ’ta devam eden Webrazzi Sessions: AI , Paribu Ürün Ekipleri Lideri Baki E r ’in sunumuyla sürüyor. Er, “ Sıfır Mesafe: Bilgi, Karar, Aksiyon ” başlıklı sunumunda katılımcılarla bir araya geldi.
Paribu Intelligence ’ın lansmanının ardından yalnızca ürünü değil, ürünün ortaya çıkış sürecini ve şirketin yapay zekayla birlikte geçirdiği dönüşümü de konuşmak istediklerini belirten Er, yapay zekaya yaklaşımlarının yalnızca kod yazmakla sınırlı olmadığını söyledi. Er, asıl meselenin yapay zekayı iş süreçlerine entegre etmek ve bu dönüşümde insanın rolünü doğru konumlandırmak olduğunu da dile getirdi.
Bu doğrultuda şirket içinde Foundation ekibini kurduklarını belirten Er, yeni ürünlerin ilk günden itibaren güvenli şekilde geliştirilmesini hedeflediklerini aktardı. Birbirinden bağımsız ekipler yerine, farklı araçları ve süreçleri ortak bir noktada buluşturan bir yapı kurmaları gerektiğini söyleyen Er, şirketin daha önce oluşturduğu framework'ün de bu dönüşümde yol gösterici olduğunu ifade etti.
Yapay zekanın ekip yapısını da değiştirdiğini belirten Er, Enablement ekibini kapattıklarını ve bu süreçte herkesin yapay zeka dönüşümüne dahil olduğunu söyledi. Yeni organizasyon yapısında ekipleri en fazla üç kişiden oluşan pod'lara ayırdıklarını da aktaran Er, yapay zeka araçlarıyla güçlenen bir geliştiricinin daha fazla sorumluluk üstlenebildiğini dile getirdi. Servis sahiplerinin kendi planları doğrultusunda özerk hareket edebilmesi için pod'lar arasında geçiş imkânı da oluşturduklarını belirtti.
Bu yeni yapının ekiplerin daha hızlı hareket etmesini ve daha fazla deneme yapmasını sağladığını söyleyen Er, ürün geliştirme sürecinde hangi verinin ölçüleceği sorusunun da daha erken gündeme geldiğini ifade etti. Bununla birlikte farklı ürünleri birbirine bağlama konusunda henüz istedikleri hıza ulaşamadıklarını da ekledi.
Yapay zeka destekli ürünlerin geliştirilme hızının beraberinde bazı zorluklar getirdiğine dikkat çeken Er, bu temponun insanları yorabildiğini söyledi. Statik bir ürünün, sürekli gelişen bir ürüne kıyasla daha az yorucu olduğunu belirten Er, uygulamaların giderek daha fazla katman kazandığını ve yapay zekanın bu katmanların tamamını anlayabilen bir yapıya dönüştüğünü dile getirdi.
Paribu Intelligence'ın da bu yaklaşımın bir parçası olduğunu belirten Baki Er, bir yatırım uygulamasında nihai kararın her zaman kullanıcıya ait olması gerektiğinin altını çizdi. Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held
Colombian police forces stormed a supermarket in Cartagena, one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, in the early hours of Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.
Far-right president Abelardo de la Espriella travelled to the Caribbean city to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.
When masked and armed criminals stormed the supermarket at about 8.30am on Tuesday, 30 people – including customers and employees – were taken hostage, many of them seen through the windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When the final 20 hostages were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday – after 17 hours in captivity – four criminals were arrested and one was killed.
In a video posted outside the supermarket – just about six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year – De la Espriella celebrated the end of the operation.
“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” he said with a gun on his waist, as he has appeared publicly on other occasions as part of his populist rhetoric on public security.
The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another criminal attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the car-bomb attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the armed criminal groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
Commenting on what he called an “extraordinary” rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The day-long hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.
In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.
Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

Bellingham has scored seven goals this season but this will be one to remember
Manager Jose Mourinho described Jude Bellingham as "without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world" following a wonder goal which inspired a brilliant second-half performance for Real Madrid in a 5-1 win against PSV .
Mourinho opted to leave the England midfielder out of the starting line-up for Tuesday's Champions League game at the Bernabeu - an understandable decision given the demands of Madrid's fixture schedule and the strength in depth at his disposal.
But after watching his side trail 1-0 at half-time against the Dutch side, Mourinho knew changes were needed.
"He is an amazing player that has everything," the Portuguese manager said. "He has physicality, he understands the game, he has absolutely everything. Today, he has changed how the game was evolving."
Captain Fede Valverde equalised in the 50th minute and 10 minutes later Bellingham produced his moment of magic.
Receiving the ball just outside the penalty area, he took two touches to lift it into position before unleashing a magnificent volley with the outside of his right foot, leaving PSV keeper Matej Kovar with no chance.
It was a sensational finish, executed with extraordinary precision.
"I was a bit surprised, honestly," Bellingham said about the goal. "I knew that I could control the ball well and get it into my grasp. But normally from there, I'm looking to see who's on as an option to play through.
"It popped up nicely and I thought I'm just going to hit it. So yeah, it was a nice goal and important for the team, being the second goal, and gave us control."
The 23-year-old celebrated in trademark fashion, standing with his arms outstretched in front of the home supporters as thousands serenaded him with chants of 'Hey Jude'.
It was his fourth goal in his past five appearances for Real.
Asked whether he should be compared to Real and France legend Zinedine Zidane, who won the Ballon d'Or and World Cup in 1998, Bellingham maintained his humility.
"I think Zidane is much better than me. He's much more elegant and he's my idol," he said.
'I'm just going to hit it!' - Bellingham reacts to stunning goal
Kylian Mbappe scored two more goals and Vinicius Junior put away the fifth to complete a super turnaround from a team that had looked short of ideas in the first half.
At the suggestion that he is currently in the form of his life, Bellingham said: "I think you're only as good as your next one [game]. Your last one doesn't really matter.
"But my focus has to change now to preparing for the next game. Thinking about my best form or being the best player in the world doesn't mean anything to me."
For Bellingham, the ability to respond when things are not going according to plan is what separates the best teams from the rest.
"We're managing to show that mentality that good teams do, that even if you're not playing well, you can raise the level at any point," he said.
His adaptation to life in Spain has also been an important part of that journey.
Asked about his increasingly impressive Spanish, Bellingham admitted he still gets nervous when speaking the language in public.
"It's getting a little bit better. I get a little bit nervous speaking to you guys. It's much easier in the changing room," he joked to journalists.
"I'm loving living in Spain. I'm loving the club. I think for English players it's such an important thing to go and move abroad and learn new things and I've obviously benefited massively from that."
And while his performances have inevitably brought renewed attention to individual awards, Bellingham said that personal recognition is not what motivates him.
Asked about the Ballon d'Or, he said his focus was only on the team.
"I don't care about the Ballon d'Or, honestly. I want to win a lot of titles with the team, the Champions League, the League."
"The Ballon d'Or is something for you, journalists, to vote and create a bit of tension. But for me it's more important that the team win."

Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded
Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.
Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said was a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.
They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.
With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, De la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, in which one gunman was killed.
Around 20 people were still being held hostage when the security forces moved in
Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers.
One was killed in the operation and four have been arrested.
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
In footage released since then, he can be seen, with a handgun strapped to his belt, flanked by the commanders of the operation.
Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused.
Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, which is located in a popular shopping mall.
Local media said that as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads.
It is not clear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.
Local media are reporting that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.
The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.
The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.
Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.
A woman called Sandra told news site Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.
Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.
Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.
But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.
Relatives and bystanders congregated outside the entrance to the supermarket
At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.
Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination with foreign and Colombian tourists.
Cartagena's mayor, Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".
President De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.
On Tuesday, he had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb which detonated outside the regional government's offices .
While De la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.

Colombia's President President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Wednesday that around 20 hostages being held by gunmen in a supermarket in Cartagena had been rescued. Security forces earlier entered the scene of the hours-long siege after several explosions were heard.
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held had been rescued and one captor killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to have been held by armed men.
"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a video posted on social media.
Shortly after midnight, a police helicopter hovered low over the shopping centre as security forces massed outside the supermarket, AFP reporters saw.
Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
About 20 hostages were believed to be inside at the time of the assault.
Ten of the roughly 30 people initially held had already been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Exito supermarket as security forces secured the building.
De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and a sidearm while brandishing a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a roaring success.
"We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively," he said.
Read more Filming among body bags: New Colombian president’s comms campaign sparks backlash
Cartagena's mayor said all the hostages were "safe and sound" and would reunite with their families before undergoing medical checks.
The siege gripped Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism.
Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.
"My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told AFP earlier in the standoff.
"He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared on social media appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear carrying long guns alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.
De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping – no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted armored vehicle robbery at the shopping center.
According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly $2 million, two armored vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 130 kilometres (80 miles) northeast of Cartagena.
The siege unfolded on the 10th anniversary of Colombia 's landmark peace accord with FARC guerrillas and a series of attacks across the country.
Despite the deal that ended the region's largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organisations still fight for control of parts of the country.
Late Monday, authorities blamed a dissident FARC faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.
Separately, the presidency said a "terrorist attack" on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several southwestern departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

Jude Bellingham admits he had ‘no idea’ what he’d done after scoring a goal that drew comparisons with Zinadine Zidane.
Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham has brushed aside comparisons with football great Zinedine Zidane following his sensational goal against PSV in the Champions League.
The England international came on at half-time with Los Blancos trailing and inspired a sensational second-half display, including a magnificent effort from distance, at the Santiago Bernabeu on Tuesday.
Bellingham said he “did not know” how he scored his brilliant goal, flicking the ball up on the edge of the box and slicing a stunning effort inside the far post.
Having seen an acrobatic volley blocked minutes earlier, the England midfielder controlled Kylian Mbappe’s pass with two touches in the air and curled a superb shot into ⁠⁠the far corner from well outside the area.
“I have no idea what I did,” Bellingham told RMTV. “I had the ball in a good position and thought about shooting.”
The 23-year-old, upon joining Real Madrid, took Zidane’s number five shirt in “homage” to the Frenchman, whom he admired, and some have compared his goal to a Zidane-style strike.
“I do things that you guys think are similar to Zidane, but he was much better than me,” Bellingham told reporters.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho hailed Bellingham’s game-changing display as the midfielder gave Mourinho credit for helping him find arguably the best form he has enjoyed at Madrid in recent weeks, with Los Blancos winning a 10th straight match, but the coach said the midfielder only had himself to thank.
“I think the main figure responsible for what Jude is today is Jude, and his teammates. I try to help a little,” said the Portuguese coach.
“He’s an absolutely extraordinary player who has everything – he has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything and today, obviously not by himself, but he changed the direction of the match.”
“He’s an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world,” Mourinho said.
Madrid’s victory over the Dutch champions maintained their 100 percent start to the league phase, in which they are provisional leaders.
Mourinho reiterated his view that it was a “scandal” that Bellingham was not ranked in the top 10 players in the world at this year’s Ballon d’Or ceremony.
Mbappe netted twice to put Real out of sight before Vinicius Jr got in on the act with a late goal, having struck the post twice earlier in the game.

After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance
A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history.
As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday , was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute.
“Correcting one injustice with another cannot be considered an acceptable response, either from a sporting or an ethical standpoint,” Sobha said. “Football is founded on core values: fairness, merit and the truth of what happens on the field. Awarding a title outside these principles, even when supported by regulatory provisions, undermines the credibility of the competition and damages the integrity of the game.
“Rather than restoring balance, such a choice risks intensifying frustrations and calls for a deeper reflection on how to safeguard fairness and uphold the honour of African football.”
Managing the huge reputational damage from the crisis over the past 10 months has been arguably the biggest governance test for the five-year Caf presidency of the South African billionaire Patrice Motsepe.
In a frustrated, exasperated moment, he admitted he was “sick and tired” of it all, navigating the treacherous diplomatic minefield of wounded Moroccan and Senegalese feelings, while reiterating his neutrality and belief in the integrity of the judicial process to bring the dispute to a just end.
The Cas resolution of the dispute compels Caf to carry out a desperately needed and long overdue task: the root-and-branch reform of its justice system, particularly the appeals board chaired by the Nigerian judge Roli Harriman.
The Cape Verdean Faustino Varela Monteiro, the board’s vice-chair, is a notable, honourable exception, standing for the correct legal position in his dissenting judgment.
The appeals board needlessly overturned the verdict of Caf’s disciplinary committee, which struck the right balance of upholding the result of the final while imposing fines and bans on the Senegal team for the egregious act of disrupting the match, and in so doing exposed its acute lack of understanding of the critical role it is duty-bound to play in the dispensation of football justice.
“You are right,” says a Caf executive committee member about the need to dissolve the appeals board and reconstitute it with jurists possessing the knowledge needed to restore confidence in the African football justice system.
Ensuring that politically exposed people are no longer members of a reconstituted appeals board is also imperative, if confidence in the impartiality of its verdicts is to be restored. No federation president should have a place on it. The presence of Moez Nasri, the president of the Tunisian Football Federation, strips it of credibility, as Motsepe acknowledged when I pointed this out to him in March.
But the poor quality of Jean-Jacques Ndala Ngambo’s refereeing of the Afcon final and Safari Olivier Kabene’s equally bad chairing of Caf’s referees committee – whose selection of match officials was responsible for the inadequate quality of game management throughout the last tournament – remain the proverbial elephants in the governance room.
When I asked a high-ranking Caf official why Ngambo has not faced a disciplinary hearing for his management of the final, he claimed its hands were tied by the Cas judicial process. That excuse expired on Tuesday.
Ngambo’s decision to allow a restart of the game, after Senegal illegally walked out for about 15 minutes in protest against a penalty awarded to Morocco, was a deeply questionable, some would say unacceptable, use of his discretionary powers, which should have leaned towards a declaration of match abandonment, with Morocco being declared the winners.
That said, the referee’s earlier failure to award Senegal what appeared to be a clear goal, subsequently giving a penalty to Morocco in second-half stoppage time, was the trigger for the chaos.
Ngambo’s lack of fortitude and experience, to cope with the demands of an Afcon final, is an indictment of the committee that picked the wrong man to handle it. And Kabene is responsible for that. “We have to do a clearout of the referees committee,” says a member of the Caf executive committee.
It is a situation in sharp and sad contrast to the world-class officiating at the 2024 Afcon in Côte d’Ivoire, under the competent general management of the Ivorian Noumandiez Doué, who would be the ideal person to restore sanity.
But after the shabby way he was treated, losing his job while on assignment at the last Championship of African Nations, for domestic-based players, in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania – the countries staging the 2027 Afcon – it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than it would be to convince him to return to his old job.
With just over eight months to the next Afcon and 20 months to the 2028 tournament, yet to have a designated host, Caf’s governance and organisational challenges are far from over.
The last two Afcons of Motsepe’s presidency, which ends in March 2029, will be decisive in shaping his legacy.

Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025
China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.
China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.
For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.
The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.
Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged .
Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.
He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.
He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.
The hashtag “Chen Jining under investigation” had amassed about 240m views on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo by Wednesday morning, with many users saying they were “shocked” and “stunned” in comments under state media posts.
“This is arguably the biggest political news to come out of China in a few years,” Taisu Zhang, a professor at Yale Law School specialising in contemporary Chinese law and politics, wrote on X.
Zhang pointed to Chen’s status as a rising political star who had been seen as “a near-lock for the politburo Standing Committee”, China’s highest political decision-making body.
At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign , which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged , including those once thought untouchable.
Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.
“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.
Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ‘self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.
The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.
Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.
“Chen Jining is no ordinary fallen official … [He is] an exemplar of someone who rose from the specialised field of environmental protection to the pinnacle of political power,” Mao Shoulong, a professor of public administration and policy at Renmin University of China, wrote in a commentary on WeChat.
“His downfall, therefore, is not merely that of an individual, but of an entire type of official, a model of political advancement, and a set of assumptions about the relationship between technology and politics, expertise and power, and competence and loyalty,” Mao wrote.
Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.
The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of country's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 12 jurisdictions affected.
The move comes after the White House's launched an investigation into the practices of its trading partners in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .
China is facing the highest rate of "up to 40%", followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.
Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to.
Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing the policy will boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
But economists have warned import taxes can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers and dampen global trade.
Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

Chen is the fourth high-ranking Politburo member to be pushed out in two years.
The Chinese Communist Party has launched investigations into the party’s Shanghai secretary Chen Jining for alleged “serious violations of discipline and law” – usually code for corruption.
The anticorruption watchdog, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, announced the probe in a brief statement on Tuesday, according to Xinhua News Agency, but did not give more details.
It comes amid widespread purges in the Political Bureau, one of the top bodies of the CCP, as the party prepares for its next congress in the second half of 2027, where President Xi Jinping is expected to clinch his fourth five-year term.
Xi, who has pushed greater party discipline and anticorruption, has for years pursued a long, intense purge on a scale not seen since the rule of Mao Zedong, experts say.
The Shanghai Communist Party’s leaders have backed the move, with its standing committee stating it firmly supported the decision to investigate Chen and that it showed Beijing’s determination to continue its anticorruption campaign.
“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anticorruption campaign has no limits,” Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, told The Associated Press news agency. “The pattern is unprecedented.” Here’s what we know:
Chen, 62, joined the CCP as a 20-year-old environmental engineering student at the highly-rated Tsinghua University. After spending a decade researching in the United Kingdom, the scientist and academic returned to Tsinghua, where he was eventually appointed one of its youngest presidents in 2012.
He went on to serve as the Minister of Environmental Protection from 2015 to 2017, and led efforts to cut pollution in Beijing. He was later appointed Mayor of Beijing in 2018.
In 2022, he was appointed party secretary of Shanghai, the country’s financial hub, amid Xi’s push to install people with strong scientific backgrounds in key roles.
Chen was widely seen as Xi’s protege. His post is usually seen as a stepping stone to party leadership; President Xi previously held the position of Shanghai Party Secretary in 2007.
Chen hosted some of China’s most prominent diplomatic visitors, including former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
He led the opening ceremony of the World AI Conference held earlier this year in Shanghai.
Other senior party officials have been purged in recent months, especially in the military.
The military shakeups and wider purge are part of Xi’s years-long anticorruption drive that has seen hundreds of senior and junior government officials investigated, prosecuted or dismissed since Xi first came to power in 2012.
Analysts believe the purges are designed to reform the military and to ensure unwavering loyalty to Xi.
Some military expulsions have been linked to suspicions of political divergence. Official sources, for example, described additional allegations against He Weidong, the former vice chairman of the military commission, as being a “loss of chastity,” a rare phrase which, in CCP speak, refers to political disloyalty and ideological collapse.
The takedowns reveal how Chinese politics often depends on shifting circumstances, with even officials possessing the qualifications Xi wants being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at the Washington-based American University.
“On paper,” they appear to be “individuals Xi would appreciate,” Torigian told the AP. But afterwards, “we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them”.

At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC.
The leaked Rosstat data reveal how the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has fundamentally changed mortality patterns in Russia, and show the high cost paid in human life in a war that Vladimir Putin had assumed would last only days but is now almost five years old.
BBC Russian has had access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarusian group Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow.
Russia's statistics agency admitted to a cyber-attack, but denied any protected information had been leaked.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that only Russia's defence ministry could officially report data on losses: "I suggest no other data be taken into account." The defence ministry has not released any official casualty figures for several years.
Together with independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian has compared the Rosstat data with its own list of confirmed military deaths, pulled from open sources since the start of the invasion, and it has found matches for 90% of the records.
Military experts estimate that the BBC's list of 290,012 deaths, gleaned from official reports, social media, new memorials and graves, may account for 45-55% of the true death toll, which would range from 527,295 to 644,471.
The records show that 65% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Russia who lost their lives in 2025 died in the war. For those aged 25-34 the number was 59%. Only among 45 to 54 year-olds does cardiovascular disease claim more Russian lives than the conflict.
The data also reveal the extent of losses in specific areas of Ukraine. Some 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of 10 Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000.
During the fight for one small village called Andriivka, south of the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk region, 1,122 Russians lost their lives. Before the war 74 people lived there.
Russia does not give public figures for losses sustained since the war began in February 2022. And two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing data of deaths from external causes, which was used to gauge the extent of military losses.
For example, only 70% of deaths we have established of soldiers from the occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk in eastern Ukraine who fought in the Russian army were accounted for in the Rosstat files.
Overall, the Rosstat dataset confirms the trends that we have observed with our own count.
Ukrainian losses were last put at about 50,000 by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July 2026, but another list based on open sources by the anonymous UA Losses website puts the figure at 115,952.
The Rosstat dataset contains no names but does include ages, places of residence, places of death and also circumstances of death.
We have filtered the records first by location, leaving only Ukraine as well as Russian border regions that saw incursions by the Ukrainian army.
Next, we identified 425,174 entries explicitly indicating a military-related cause of death, such as explosions or shrapnel during combat operations.
As this count could include civilians, we filtered out women as well as men outside the 18-65 age group. And if someone lived and died in the four Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, we excluded them as a possible civilian – unless he had a record of military service attached to his entry.
Another 14,093 entries were identified by looking at employment, and 51,067 were recorded in the database as deceased on the basis of a court ruling. This often happens when a soldier goes missing in a combat zone for more than six months and their body has not been recovered.
Again, we filtered out civilians by only counting deaths in the war zones in Ukraine and Russia.
According to BBC Russian's analysis of the leaked files, in the first year of the war the average age of those killed was 34. By 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers entered the ranks, it had risen to 40 (38 according to our own list).
Some of Russia's poorest regions in Eastern Siberia account for a disproportionately large share of the losses. Men from Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai are 20-25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of the biggest cities of Moscow and St Petersburg.
In most regions, the distribution of deaths based on Rosstat data differs from that in the BBC's list by just a few tenths of a percentage point.
At least 5,017 foreigners are among those who died fighting for Russia, according to our analysis of the Rosstat files, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. We have left out Ukrainians from this count to avoid including civilians.
This is a conservative estimate as dual nationals are listed as Russians in the database, and there is no reference to North Koreans who died repelling the Ukrainian incursion into Russia in 2024.
The BBC identified 2,304 North Korean soldiers who died there by analysing satellite imagery and official photographs of a newly built memorial in Pyongyang.
The leaked Russian statistics may not be complete but taken in conjunction with BBC Russian's own work they are significant.
In the context of a war that has lasted four years and 10 months, these are high numbers for Russia, when compared with the Soviet war in Afghanistan that ended in 1989.
In that 10-year war, an estimated 15,000 Red Army troops died, and an estimated one million civilians were killed.

Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics
The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.
At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing .
There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.
On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.
Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.
He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".
Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.
"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."
"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."
On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.
"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.
The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.
It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.
Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.
"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.
William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".
Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.
Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.
The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.
Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.
Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China .

Solomon Islands will have to consult Canberra before making new security or infrastructure deals under new pact.
Solomon Islands and Australia have signed a sweeping treaty affirming that the small Pacific country will allow no foreign military bases on its territory.
The deal, signed on Wednesday, is seen as a blow to the regional ambitions of China, which had been moving closer to the Solomon Islands for years.
“Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are gone,” Prime Minister Matthew Wale told journalists alongside his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese.
The treaty establishes Australia as the island nation’s “primary security partner” and will see Canberra provide 740 million Australian dollars ($490m) over the next 10 years to fund free education and other programmes in Solomon Islands. Solomon Islands has a gross domestic product (GDP) of $1.75bn, according to the World Bank.
In exchange, Solomon Islands will allow no foreign military or security bases on its soil, and the country’s “sensitive” infrastructure will “remain free from militarisation, foreign interference and unauthorised access”.
That includes ports, airports, energy and telecommunications, as well as road and bridge construction – areas China has dominated in the islands through its Belt and Road Initiative. The deal will not apply retroactively.
Solomon Islands will also have to consult Australia before making deals involving its critical infrastructure or security cooperation unless it is with members of the Pacific Islands Forum regional bloc, Albanese said.
Since being elected in May, Wale has upended Solomon Islands’ diplomatic moves towards China and realigned with Australia and the United States.
Asked about reports he had ended a secretive security pact with Beijing, Wale told journalists that discussions with China were “ongoing”.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not confirm whether the deal had been scrapped, but warned that the new agreement with Australia “should not target any third party”.
This is the latest in a string of similar deals Australia has struck with Pacific states, including Papua New Guinea , Vanuatu and Fiji .

Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.
The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.
Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.
Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.
Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

Divers recover bodies after Cessna 210 went down in Gulf of Mexico on Tuesday afternoon killing all onboard
Divers have found the bodies of six people killed in a small plane crash on Tuesday off the coast of Mississippi, according to the US Coast Guard.
Their bodies were in the plane’s fuselage after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi , and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands national seashore. Four adults and two boys, ages eight and 10, were onboard, a Coast Guard spokesperson, Juan Ros, said.
The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported about 3.45pm that it lost contact with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard. Responders searched for hours and initially only found three lifejackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to Ros.
The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard coordinator for search and rescue in the Mobile area, called the situation heartbreaking.
“While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency coordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families,” he said in a statement.
The New Orleans news station WVUE reported that those onboard the crashed plane were traveling back home after a fishing trip in Venice, Louisiana.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will investigate the crash.
On 3 November, a Learjet 60 business jet nosedived into the ground in south Florida, killing all nine people on board. The terrifying crash was captured on video recorded by people inside their cars.

Salvadorian man, who was deported in March 2025 and returned to US after supreme court ruling, leaving of own volition for Spain
Kilmar Ábrego García has left the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday, with the Department of Homeland Security confirming that he was travelling to Spain.
A source close to Ábrego said Madrid was his first stop but that it would not be his final destination.
The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison .
He was ultimately returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.
In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.
“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”
The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.
He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego García for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.
“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego García’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post . “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
Additional reporting by Ashifa Kassam in Madrid and the Associated Press

It is unclear how long Kilmar Ábrego García will stay in Spain for
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, has arrived in Spain from the US.
After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".
"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.
"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."
The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.
Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.
In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.
The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, India remains vulnerable to erratic monsoons
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks , external are particularly ample.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.
Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis , external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.
India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

FILE - Senegal's Sadio Mane holds the trophy aloft as he celebrates with teammates after winning the Africa Cup of Nations final soccer match between Senegal and Morocco in Rabat, Morocco, Sunday, Jan. 18, 2026. Youssef Loulidi/AP hide caption
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.
The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.
Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."
Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.
"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."
Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.
In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.
The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.
Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."
CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.
Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.
Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.
The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).
Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.
Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.
The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.
Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.
Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.
The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.
In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."
The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.
The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.
"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.
Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.
"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.
"At the end of the day Morocco and Senegal are brothers," Sidibé added, referring to the countries' long shared close ties built on religion, trade and culture.
Sidi Sylla, a philosophy student at Dakar's main university, said the court's ruling was "not just a win for Senegal but for football in general."
CAS rulings have stripped many athletes of Olympic medals for doping, but it's rare to overturn the result of a major soccer competition.
CAS refused to change the results of the 2019 Asian Cup, dismissing an appeal that the star striker on winning team Qatar shouldn't have been eligible for the tournament.
A lengthy legal battle over the same year's African Champions League final also ended with the original winner, Esperance of Tunisia, taking the title after its opponent Wydad from Morocco refused to play on.
One notable CAS ruling on a team sport title came at the Winter Olympics in 2022. A doping case involving then-15-year-old Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva ended up with her disqualification, and the Russian team being dropped from gold to bronze in the team event.
